reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Bleeding is broadly classified as anterior or posterior, which differ in likely source, severity and management
Most bleeds are anterior and arise from Little's area on the nasal septum, where several vessels anastomose (Kiesselbach's plexus)
Posterior bleeds tend to occur in older patients, are more profuse, and are harder to control, with a higher risk of airway soiling and significant blood loss
Causes are grouped into local (trauma, digital picking, foreign body, infection, tumour) and general (hypertension, coagulopathy, anticoagulants, hereditary telangiectasia)
First aid principles are sitting upright, leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose, with attention to airway and circulation
Stepwise management progresses from cautery of an identified bleeding point to anterior packing and then posterior packing or balloon devices
Refractory bleeding may require endoscopic or surgical arterial ligation or embolisation of the offending vessel
Unilateral persistent or recurrent bleeding, especially with nasal obstruction, warrants evaluation for a tumour such as juvenile angiofibroma in adolescent males
reference.pathophysiology: Epistaxis is bleeding from the nasal mucosa, whose rich, superficial vascular supply from branches of both the internal and external carotid systems makes it prone to haemorrhage. Anterior bleeding usually comes from the low-pressure anastomotic vessels of Little's area, provoked by drying, trauma or minor mucosal injury. Posterior bleeding tends to arise from larger branches such as the sphenopalatine artery and is aggravated by hypertension and vascular fragility in older patients. Systemic factors such as bleeding disorders, anticoagulation and platelet dysfunction impair haemostasis and prolong or worsen bleeding.
additionalDifferentials: Bleeding from a nasal or sinonasal tumour
Haemoptysis or upper gastrointestinal bleeding mimicking nasal bleeding
Trauma including base of skull fracture with CSF or blood
additionalInvestigations: Anterior rhinoscopy and nasal endoscopy to localise the bleeding point
Blood pressure measurement and assessment of haemodynamic status
Full blood count, coagulation profile and group and save or crossmatch in significant bleeds
Review of anticoagulant and antiplatelet medication
Imaging (CT or MRI) and referral where a sinonasal tumour or vascular lesion is suspected
redFlags: Profuse or posterior bleeding with hypovolaemia or haemodynamic instability requiring resuscitation
Airway compromise from blood aspiration in heavy or bilateral bleeding
Bleeding uncontrolled by packing needing arterial ligation or embolisation
Recurrent unilateral bleeding with a mass suggesting malignancy or angiofibroma
reference.prognosis: Most anterior nosebleeds settle with simple first aid or cautery, whereas posterior and recurrent bleeds, particularly in patients with hypertension or coagulopathy, can be severe or life-threatening and may need aggressive intervention.
pitfalls: Failing to assess and resuscitate the patient while focusing only on the nose
Overlooking a posterior source when anterior examination appears clear
Missing an underlying tumour in recurrent unilateral bleeding
Neglecting to review anticoagulation and correct coagulopathy
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
